title: Count Animation Frames | Design Game Feel with Timing

scenes.title: Turn Feel into Timing
lines: Make the attack a little faster. It is a familiar request during development.
Should we shorten the preparation, or the pause after impact?
Consider a jump in Mega Man 11 or an attack in Monster Hunter Rise.
One action contains a beginning, a change, and an ending.
We will translate that feeling into a time scale measured in frames.
The games illustrate observable motion.
We will verify exact numbers in an original frame-timing test.
The number of drawings is not necessarily the game’s time scale.

scenes.title: A Frame Count Needs a Reference Rate
lines: Set the reference rate before saying how many frames an action takes.
At sixty steps per second, twelve frames represent zero point two seconds.
At thirty steps per second, the same twelve frames represent zero point four seconds.
The count stays the same, but the elapsed time doubles.
Our test therefore uses a fixed sixty-update-per-second rule.
It displays elapsed time alongside a moving marker.
Record the frame count and its reference rate together in your design notes.
Rendering and game-rule updates can run at different rates.

scenes.title: Define the Interval You Measure
lines: Now decide which part of an attack you are measuring.
Our original test records input acceptance as time zero.
The hit area begins after twelve time steps,
stays active for three steps, then recovers for fifteen.
The total is thirty steps, or zero point five seconds.
If the request for speed concerns preparation,
we can shorten that phase and keep the others unchanged.
Record both boundaries so everyone measures the same interval.
These prototype numbers do not represent move data from another game.

scenes.title: Pose Clock and Collision Clock
lines: Does adding drawings make the hit happen sooner?
We changed only the poses in the same attack.
One version holds fewer poses longer; the other changes poses more often.
Both hit areas begin at the same twelfth time step.
Their visual smoothness differs, but the wait for the hit is equal.
We distinguish the animation-pose clock from the hit-area clock.
Before adding poses, decide which timing you want to change.
The implementation and logs verify that poses and collision timing are separate.

scenes.title: Which Clock Includes the Pause?
lines: Next, examine a brief pause at impact.
In our test, only the combat clock pauses for four steps after collision.
The background time indicator keeps moving.
The attack data still spans thirty combat steps,
but the actual completion time also includes the pause.
When observing a paused action, ask which clock the count refers to.
This does not imply that every commercial game uses this method.
It illustrates explicitly choosing what pauses and what continues in our own game.

scenes.title: Observe First, Then Verify with Logs
lines: Finally, frames counted in a recording are only one kind of evidence.
Repeated or missing pictures can obscure the game’s internal timing.
Even at different display update rates,
the same fixed hit-area clock produces the hit at the same elapsed time.
First, watch at normal speed and estimate the duration.
Then record input acceptance, the first active hit, and when another action is allowed.
Check the reference rate alongside the measured elapsed time
to turn a vague request for speed into a change everyone can review.
Find it by feel, then verify it by measurement.
